question: During a school health check, a 9-year-old girl has a BMI-for-age at the 88th percentile. Her father has type 2 diabetes and her mother is obese. She watches 5 hours of TV daily and has a diet high in sugary snacks. Which risk category best describes her, and what is the priority intervention?

answers.text: She is currently normal weight; no intervention is warranted until BMI crosses the 95th percentile.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Her BMI at the 88th percentile classifies her as overweight. Combined with multiple high-risk factors (family history of diabetes and obesity, high screen time, poor diet), a structured preventive intervention is indicated now — not at the threshold for obesity.

answers.text: High-risk overweight child; priority is pharmacological appetite suppression to prevent progression to obesity.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Pharmacotherapy is NOT the first-line intervention for a 9-year-old overweight child. Lifestyle modification (dietary change, physical activity increase, screen-time reduction) and family-centred counselling are the evidence-based primary interventions.

answers.text: High-risk overweight child; priority is family-centred lifestyle modification targeting diet quality, physical activity, and screen-time reduction.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This child is overweight (BMI-for-age 85th–94th percentile) with multiple risk factors (parental obesity/diabetes, sedentary behaviour, poor dietary quality). The evidence-based priority is a risk-stratified, family-centred lifestyle intervention — not pharmacotherapy or bariatric referral at this stage.

answers.text: Bariatric surgical referral should be initiated immediately because parental diabetes confers an irreversible metabolic trajectory.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Bariatric surgery has very limited indications in paediatric obesity (typically severe obesity with life-threatening comorbidities in adolescents, not a 9-year-old overweight child). Family-centred lifestyle intervention is the appropriate starting point.

overallFeedback.feedback: For an overweight child with multiple risk factors, the risk-stratified prevention approach centres on family-centred lifestyle modification (diet, activity, screen-time). Pharmacotherapy and surgery are later-step interventions for severe obesity.
Correct. A risk-stratified, family-centred lifestyle intervention is the evidence-based first response for a high-risk overweight child — well before pharmacotherapy or surgery.
